author: rti_admin
title: Selective Ritual Reform and Buddhist Marriage Among Ambedkarites in Odisha
content:
Abstract: Marriage rituals in South Asia have historically reinforced caste and gender hierarchies. Within contemporary Ambedkarite Buddhist communities in Odisha, debates over “mixed marriages” frequently centre on visible Hindu practices such as Brahmin priests, sindur , and the mangalsutra . Drawing on Ambedkarite social media discussions, wedding practices, B. R. Ambedkar’s writings, and anthropological studies of marriage, this article argues that such critiques are often selective. While many Ambedkarites reject Brahmanical symbols, they continue practices such as the baraat , engagement rituals such as Nadia Dhara ( ring ceremonies), status matching in partner selection, and competitive wedding display. These practices reproduce caste, gender, and status hierarchies in new forms. This article argues that Ambedkarite Buddhist marriage remains an evolving social project. Its transformative potential depends on changing the social relations that organise marriage, not simply replacing Brahmanical symbols. It calls on Dalit Bahujan communities to reimagine Buddhist marriage as an ethical practice grounded in equality, solidarity, and collective uplift.

title: Ambedkar on the Banner, DMK in the Blueprint: What VCK’s Cabinet Berth Really Tests
content:
For the first time in its history, the Viduthalai Chiruthaigal Katchi (VCK) has a minister sitting in a Tamil Nadu Cabinet it did not help elect as the senior partner. Vanni Arasu’s appointment as the state’s first-ever Minister for Social Justice, with charge of Adi Dravidar Welfare and Hill Tribes, is being read, reasonably, as a landmark. Asked how he felt about it, Vanni Arasu called it “our dream,” telling South First that after thirty-seven years since VCK’s founding, the party finally felt it was moving toward the very purpose for which it was created. This is a remarkable admission given that, as he recalled, VCK had spent its first years boycotting elections altogether under the slogan “None of you are honest; our votes are for no one,” before Dr. Thirumavalavan steered the movement toward the ballot. That is the image. An Ambedkarite reading of this moment has to ask what this implies.

Dr. Ambedkar did not write in the abstract about representation. He fought, lost, and wrote about a specific question: when a numerically small, historically oppressed group enters a political arrangement with a numerically and socially dominant one, on whose terms does that arrangement run?

author: rti_admin
title: The Architecture of Trust: What Manipur Teaches us About Democracy, Conflict, and the Long Road to Peace
content:
When societies experience prolonged conflict, the most visible losses are often the easiest to count. We record the number of lives lost, the homes destroyed, the families displaced, and the schools that fall silent. These figures matter because they remind us of the scale of human suffering. Yet they reveal only part of the story. Every conflict also destroys something far less visible but infinitely more difficult to rebuild: trust.

Trust leaves no ruins for cameras to capture. It cannot be measured in relief camps or reconstructed with bricks and concrete. Yet, it is the invisible architecture upon which every democratic society depends. It is what allows citizens to believe that institutions will protect them, that laws will be applied fairly, that differences can be resolved peacefully, and that tomorrow can be planned with a reasonable expectation of safety. Like the foundation of a building, trust often goes unnoticed until it begins to crack. When that invisible architecture weakens, the consequences extend far beyond the conflict itself.

This is perhaps the most enduring lesson that Manipur offers—not only to India, but to every democracy struggling to hold together during moments of deep social division.

author: rti_admin
title: Why ‘Cocktail 2’ Still Punishes Women’s Desire Despite Pretending to be Progressive
content:
Neeraj Bunkar & Ratnapriya Singh

Bollywood has long projected itself as a space that embraces modernity. Over the years, Hindi cinema has increasingly shown women drinking alcohol, living independently, pursuing careers, entering live-in relationships, and openly discussing intimacy. Yet, beneath these seemingly progressive images, many films continue to uphold deeply conservative ideas about gender. Women who conform to emotional stability and domestic respectability are rewarded, while women who openly express desire are often framed as disruptive or morally questionable. Cocktail 2 becomes the latest example of this contradiction.

Directed by Homi Adajania and written by Tarun Jain and Luv Ranjan, Cocktail 2 revisits familiar territory: urban relationships, friendship, attraction, and emotional betrayal among young cosmopolitan Indians. At first glance, the film appears to engage with contemporary questions about trust, commitment, and intimacy in long-term relationships. But beneath its polished visuals and modern relationship dynamics lies a familiar patriarchal structure, one that continues disciplining female desire while idealizing male virtue.

Bollywood’s Familiar Formula in a New Packaging
